content:
According to 404 Media, Magnet Forensics says it has found a way to bypass an iPhone security feature that causes the device to automatically restart when it has not been unlocked for more than 72 hours. Here are the details.

Some background

The Inactivity Reboot feature, introduced in the iOS 18.1 update released nearly two years ago, forces an iPhone to restart if it has not been unlocked for more than 72 hours.

Basically, this feature makes it harder for law enforcement and forensic tools to access data on a locked iPhone, because a reboot returns the device to a "Before First Unlock" (BFU) state rather than staying in the more permissive "After First Unlock" (AFU) state.

When an iPhone is in BFU state, some sensitive data remains protected by an encryption key that can only be accessed after the user enters their passcode for the first time, at which point the device enters AFU state.

After that, more data on the device becomes accessible, until the iPhone reboots again, at which point it returns to BFU state.

The iPhone's automatic restart means that even if a device is seized by law enforcement, it may have already returned to BFU state before investigators can access it, because obtaining a search warrant or transporting the device to a forensic lab takes time.

When iOS 18.1 was released, 404 Media noted that the feature also makes it harder for thieves or other bad actors to keep a stolen iPhone in AFU state long enough to develop or use an exploit.

Report: GrayKey has successfully bypassed the Inactivity Reboot feature

404 Media reported today that, according to an "educational and instructional video made for law enforcement that appears to be dated early 2025," Magnet Forensics, the developer of the GrayKey phone-unlocking tool, appears to have developed a method to bypass the iPhone's Inactivity Reboot feature.

The report says Magnet has developed a new device called GrayKey Preserve, and has also added an "Evidence Preservation Mode" to its existing GrayKey hardware.

Both are reportedly designed to maintain the iPhone's forensic state without immediately exposing the data stored on the device, allowing law enforcement to keep that state intact while waiting for search authorisation.

The report notes that although the video does not detail the technical principles behind the bypass method, it does explain that GrayKey can keep an iPhone in AFU state even after it restarts.

Excerpts from the report:

404 Media reached out to Apple and Magnet Forensics for comment; neither responded to a request for comment. They also consulted iPhone security researcher Jiska Classen, who said Magnet may have found a way to manipulate the iPhone's clock, or simply disable the related processes that cause some data to expire.

Although the video appears to be from early 2025, it is unknown how long this technique has been in the hands of law enforcement, whether it has actually been used in investigations, and whether it still works against the latest version of iOS.
